title: Readyon Builds Four Layer Tenant Isolation for Multi Tenant Amazon EKS
gist: ReadyOn detailed a four-layer tenant isolation design for its Harmony workforce platform on shared Amazon EKS (namespaces, dedicated Karpenter node pools, per-tenant security groups, dedicated Aurora clusters), treating layers as overlapping defenses; commenters argue isolation without matching observability is false confidence.

insights.claim: ReadyOn's Harmony platform combines Kubernetes namespaces, dedicated Karpenter node pools, VPC security groups and per-tenant Aurora databases to limit cross-tenant access at the Kubernetes, compute, network and data layers while keeping a shared EKS environment.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Shared clusters with layered isolation trade some cost efficiency for lower blast radius, a template for regulated SaaS handling payroll data.
insights.locator: ReadyOn has detailed a four-layer tenant isolation

insights.claim: Layer one gives each tenant a namespace with RBAC, quotas, admission controls and default-deny network policies, generated from Git by Argo CD ApplicationSets that automatically reconcile unauthorized changes.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: GitOps enforcement makes baseline isolation drift-resistant across many tenants.
insights.locator: The first layer uses a dedicated Kubernetes namespace

insights.claim: Layer two uses a dual taint strategy in which pods must tolerate both a tenant-identifying taint and a workload-type taint, and an admission controller verifies that requested tolerations match the namespace's tenant.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Admission-checked tolerations stop a compromised workload from scheduling onto another tenant's nodes.

insights.claim: Layer three enforces below Kubernetes with per-tenant VPC security groups restricting database connections to the tenant node pool, and a private EKS API endpoint reached via VPN, OpenID Connect and multi-factor authentication.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Cloud-network controls remain effective even if Kubernetes-level policy is bypassed.
insights.locator: The third layer moves enforcement below Kubernetes

insights.claim: Layer four separates tenant data through dedicated Aurora clusters rather than row-level filtering in a shared database, plus tenant-scoped Secrets Manager paths, short-lived credentials through IAM Roles for Service Accounts and dedicated observability backends.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Database-per-tenant raises cost but removes a whole class of cross-tenant query bugs.
insights.locator: The fourth layer separates tenant data

insights.claim: ReadyOn maps controls to a 10-stage multi-tenant threat model focused on lateral movement from a compromised tenant workload and says adversarial exercises have not produced a successful cross-tenant path to date.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A self-reported negative result; absence of found paths is not proof of isolation.

insights.claim: Moving from single-tenant to multi-tenant clusters fundamentally changes the threat model, since single-tenant hardening is well documented but shared infrastructure adds new attack paths.
insights.speaker: William Antonio G
insights.so_what: Multi-tenant platforms need a separate security design effort, not just hardened clusters.
insights.quote: But when you add multi-tenancy, the threat model fundamentally changes.
insights.locator: For single-tenant clusters, hardening is a well-documented challenge

insights.claim: AWS documentation notes that namespaces, RBAC, quotas and network policies provide only logical isolation and do not stop workloads sharing nodes, recommending node selectors, affinity rules or taints and tolerations for stronger separation.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Namespace-only multi-tenancy is insufficient for sensitive data, validating the compute-layer controls.
insights.locator: AWS documentation notes that Kubernetes namespaces

insights.claim: Isolation depth without observability depth is indistinguishable from false confidence, so traces should connect workload identity with database and network enforcement to expose gaps between controls.
insights.speaker: Juan Pablo Gaviria
insights.so_what: Verification tooling is as important as the controls and a likely investment area for platform teams.
insights.quote: Isolation depth without observability depth is indistinguishable from false confidence.
insights.locator: Juan Pablo Gaviria, an engineer who commented

insights.claim: Stanford's Mohammad Akbarpour described the broader challenge as pushing AI capabilities forward while making boundaries around inaccessible data and workflows difficult to cross.
insights.speaker: Mohammad Akbarpour
insights.so_what: As AI is added to enterprise platforms, data-boundary enforcement becomes a product requirement.
insights.quote: pushing AI capabilities forward while making the boundaries around inaccessible data and workflows difficult to cross.
